abstract:
Every result in the Transport Papers is stated in one algebra: the geometric algebra of a space of directions with a rule for their square lengths. [[t]] This trail walks through its core, from that one rule to rotors, the classification of the real algebras, and the fermion Fock space. [[t]]

Products of basis directions form a basis of the whole algebra, even when some directions have zero length. [[c:std-algebra.blade-basis]] Sandwiching between directions carries out every reflection and rotation, and each rotation comes from exactly two rotors, $R$ and $-R$. [[c:std-algebra.spin-double-cover]]

Pairs of light-like directions behave exactly like fermion creation and annihilation operators. [[c:std-algebra.witt-basis-car]]
introduction: The walk starts with the defining rule, builds up grades and symmetries, and ends where the algebra meets quantum theory. [[t]]
i:standard-algebra: These results build the geometric algebra from one rule and show what it contains. [[t]]
t:^>std-algebra.vector-squares:
The algebra has a single defining rule: a vector $v$ multiplied by itself gives its square length $Q(v)$, a plain number. [[c:std-algebra.vector-squares]]

Applying that rule to a sum of two vectors $u$ and $v$ gives \[ uv + vu = 2B(u, v), \] where $B$ is the dot product that $Q$ defines. [[c:std-algebra.vector-squares]] So the product $uv$ is the scalar $B(u, v)$ plus a part that changes sign when the order is swapped. [[c:std-algebra.vector-squares]]
t:std-algebra.vector-squares>std-algebra:
Reordering costs only a sign and a scalar, and a repeated vector collapses to a number, so every product reduces to products $e_I$ of distinct basis vectors in increasing order. [[c:std-algebra.blade-basis]]

In $n$ dimensions these blades, from $1$ up to the full volume, form a basis, so \[ \dim \Cl(V, Q) = 2^{n} \] [[c:std-algebra.blade-basis]] This holds when some directions have zero length, which matters because the series works in exactly such degenerate spaces. [[c:std-algebra.blade-basis]]
t:std-algebra.blade-basis>std-algebra.in:
Each blade has a grade $k$, the number of vectors in it, so every element splits into scalars, vectors, bivectors and so on. [[c:std-algebra.involution-properties]]

Three ways of flipping an element act on grade $k$ by a sign: the grade involution, reversion (writing every product backwards) and their composite. [[c:std-algebra.involution-properties]] Reversion, written with a tilde, acts by \[ \tilde{x} = (-1)^{k(k-1)/2} x \] on grade $k$, and it is the one that undoes rotations later in the walk. [[c:std-algebra.involution-properties]]
t:std-algebra.involution-properties>prim:
The elements that commute with everything form the centre of the algebra. [[t]]

With $n$ even only the scalars are central. [[c:primer.centre]] With $n$ odd the pseudoscalar $\omega = e_1 e_2 \cdots e_n$, the product of all the basis vectors, is central too. [[c:primer.centre]]

Whether the pseudoscalar squares to plus or minus one decides much of the algebra's shape, as the classification below shows. [[t]]
t:primer.centre>std-algebra.reflection:
A vector $u$ with $Q(u) \ne 0$ can be divided by. [[c:std-algebra.reflection]] Sandwiching another vector $x$ between it and its inverse gives \[ x \mapsto -u x u^{-1}, \] the reflection in the mirror perpendicular to $u$. [[c:std-algebra.reflection]]

So the algebra does geometry directly: a mirror is just a vector. [[t]]
t:std-algebra.reflection>std-algebra.spi:
Two reflections in a row give a rotation, or a boost in spacetime, and the product of the two vectors is a rotor $R$. [[c:std-algebra.spin-double-cover]] A rotor acts on vectors by \[ x \mapsto R x \tilde{R} \] [[c:std-algebra.spin-double-cover]]

In a nondegenerate space every such rotation arises this way, and exactly two rotors, $R$ and $-R$, give the same one. [[c:std-algebra.spin-double-cover]] This doubling is where spinors come from. [[t]]
t:std-algebra.spin-double-cover>std-alge:
Light-like vectors, nonzero vectors with $Q(u) = 0$, cannot be divided by, but they come in pairs. [[c:std-algebra.witt-decomposition]]

A light-like vector $u$ and a partner $w$ span a hyperbolic plane, and the space splits into as many such planes as possible: \[ V = H_1 \perp \dots \perp H_m \perp A \perp \operatorname{rad} V, \] with $m = \min(p, q)$ and $A$ free of light-like vectors. [[c:std-algebra.witt-decomposition]]

The number of these planes is the Witt index, which later in the lab counts quantum capacity. [[t]]
t:std-algebra.witt-decomposition>std-alg:
Adding one hyperbolic plane doubles the matrix size: \[ \Cl(p{+}1, q{+}1) \cong \Mat_2(\Cl(p,q)) \] [[c:std-algebra.periodicity]]

Adding eight positive or eight negative directions gives sixteen-by-sixteen matrices over the old algebra. [[c:std-algebra.periodicity]] So every real geometric algebra is a matrix algebra over $\R$, $\C$ or $\HH$, or a sum of two such, fixed by $n = p + q$ and by $p - q$ modulo $8$. [[c:std-algebra.periodicity]]
t:std-algebra.periodicity>std-algebra.wi:
Return now to the light-like pairs of a hyperbolic plane. [[t]]

Chosen as a Witt basis $v_i$, $w_i$, with $B(v_i, w_j) = \tfrac12 \delta_{ij}$, they satisfy \[ v_i w_j + w_j v_i = \delta_{ij}, \] and the $v_i$ anticommute among themselves, as do the $w_i$. [[c:std-algebra.witt-basis-car]] These are the canonical anticommutation relations, with $v_i$ annihilating and $w_i$ creating a fermion. [[c:std-algebra.witt-basis-car]]

One rule about square lengths therefore already contains the algebra of fermions. [[t]]
t:std-algebra.witt-basis-car>std-algebra:
Let the $w_i$ act by adding a direction and the $v_i$ by removing one. [[c:std-algebra.fock-representation]] This writes the whole algebra as matrices on all combinations of the $w_i$: \[ \Cl(V, Q) \cong \End(\Lambda W) \] [[c:std-algebra.fock-representation]]

That space is the fermion Fock space, and it sits inside the algebra as the left ideal generated by the vacuum idempotent $f$, so states and operators live in one algebra. [[c:std-algebra.fock-representation]]
conclusion:
From the single rule $v^{2} = Q(v)$ the walk has reached rotors, the classification of every real geometric algebra, and the fermion Fock space. [[c:std-algebra.vector-squares]]

The trail rests on no postulate. [[t]] Each step is proved in the lab and checked by machine, citing the classical law of inertia and the theorem that every isometry is a product of reflections. [[t]]
